terms.definition: Originally a Greek derogatory term for low or fraudulent magic (sorcery/witchcraft); in the Lemegeton, the name of the first book, concerned with the 72 spirits and their evocation. Contrasted with theurgy (high/divine magic).

From Greek θεουργία, 'divine working' — ritual practices associated with invoking deities or beneficent spirits, especially to achieve henosis (union with the divine) and self-perfection. Considered 'high magic' as opposed to goetia.
The Lesser Key of Solomon; a five-part grimoire compilation, of which the Ars Goetia is the first part.

A drawn symbol or character associated with a specific spirit, used in the text as a lamen (a wearable emblem) or as part of the ceremonial apparatus. The De Laurence edition contains 200 diagrams and seals.
A seal or character worn by the practitioner (e.g., before the breast or face), described in the text as something the spirit 'obeys' or requires to be shown.
A count of subordinate spirits under a given demon's government (e.g., '66 Legions of Infernal Spirits'). Counts differ between demons and between manuscript variants.
The brazen vessel in which Solomon is said to have bound the 72 spirits with their legions, sealed with the Secret Seal of Solomon, and cast into a deep lake or hole in Babylon.
A circle (described as 9 feet across) inscribed with divine names, within which the practitioner stands for protection; described in the text, not as an instruction to the reader.
A triangle (described as 3 feet across, placed 2 feet from the circle) into which spirits are said to be commanded; the base nearest the circle, apex pointing toward the spirit's quarter.
A five-pointed figure described as made in gold or silver and worn on the breast, with the spirit's seal on the reverse; said to preserve the practitioner and command spirits.
A six-pointed figure described as made on calf-skin parchment, worn at the skirt of a white vestment, and shown to spirits so they take human shape.
The seal said to have been used to bind and seal the spirits in the Vessel of Brass; the text gives elaborate (descriptive) specifications for its making.
Amaymon, Corson, Zimimay (or Ziminair), and Göap — said to rule the four cardinal quarters (East, West, North, South) and to govern all 72 spirits; not to be called except on great occasions.
One of the Four Great Kings; ruler of the East; Asmoday is described as 'first and choicest under the Power of AMAYMON', and Seere is 'under AMAYMON, King of the East'.

terms.term: Order of Virtues / Thrones / Dominations / Powers / Potentates / Angels
terms.definition: Angelological ranks (celestial orders) from which certain demons are said to have fallen; e.g., Agares 'was of the Order of Virtues', Paimon 'of the Order of Dominations', Purson's legions are 'partly of the Order of Virtues and partly of the Order of Thrones'.
Johann Weyer's demonology (in De praestigiis daemonum), commonly cited as the attributed source for the Goetia's catalogue, despite the Solomonic attribution.
Union with the divine; the goal of theurgy in Neoplatonic thought.
Practical or 'wonder-working' magic; the other major branch of the magical arts alongside theurgy.
A lead tablet inscribed with a victim's name and formulas, buried in or near a tomb or battlefield to deliver the victim to underworld powers; Greco-Roman context, not part of the Goetia itself.

source: De Laurence 1916; Goetia (magic) — Wikipedia; Theurgy — Wikipedia; Magic in the Greco-Roman world — Wikipedia
